hrZones.metaTitle: Heart rate zone calculator (%HRmax, Karvonen, LTHR) | Peakr
hrZones.metaDescription: Calculate your five heart rate training zones with the %HRmax, Karvonen (heart rate reserve) or LTHR method. Free, no account needed.
hrZones.title: Heart rate zones
hrZones.description: Your five training zones from max, resting or threshold heart rate.
hrZones.lead: Calculate your five training zones with the method that fits what you know about your heart rate.

methodInfo.percentMax: Zones as a percentage of your maximum heart rate. Simple and a good start.
methodInfo.karvonen: Uses your heart rate reserve (max minus resting). More personal, because it reflects your fitness.
methodInfo.lthr: Zones from your lactate threshold heart rate (Joe Friel). The most precise if you know your threshold.

hrZones.autoMethod: Chosen automatically: Karvonen as soon as you enter your resting heart rate.
hrZones.hrMaxEstimateNote: Estimated from your age (208 − 0.7 × age). A measured value makes your zones more accurate.

seo.heading: What are heart rate zones?
seo.body: Heart rate zones split your effort into five ranges, from very easy recovery (Zone 1) to all-out efforts (Zone 5). Training in the right zone makes sure easy days stay easy and hard days are hard enough to make you faster.

seo.heading: Which method should I use?
seo.body: %HRmax only needs your maximum heart rate (or your age for an estimate). Karvonen also uses your resting heart rate, so the zones reflect your fitness. LTHR, based on your lactate threshold heart rate from a 30-minute time trial, is the most precise for trained athletes.

seo.heading: How accurate is the age formula?
seo.body: The formula 208 − 0.7 × age is a population average – your real maximum can be 10–15 beats higher or lower. If you have seen a higher value at the end of an all-out effort, enter it as your max heart rate.

zone2.metaDescription: Find your Zone 2 heart rate range for easy aerobic training – with or without resting heart rate. Free, no account needed.
zone2.title: Zone 2 calculator
zone2.description: Find your easy aerobic range – and why it matters.
zone2.lead: Find the heart rate range for easy aerobic training – the foundation of every endurance plan.

benefits.base: Builds your aerobic base: more mitochondria and capillaries, so you get faster at the same heart rate.
benefits.fat: Trains your body to burn fat efficiently, which saves carbohydrates for hard efforts.
benefits.recovery: Easy enough to recover from quickly, so you can train more often without getting injured.
benefits.volume: Most endurance athletes do around 80 % of their training at this easy intensity.

zone2.restingHint: With resting heart rate the Karvonen method is used – more personal.

methodNote.percentMax: 60–70 % of your max heart rate ({{hrMax}} bpm).
methodNote.karvonen: 60–70 % of your heart rate reserve (Karvonen, max {{hrMax}} bpm).
methodNote.lthr: Based on your threshold heart rate.

zone2.talkTest: Check: you can still talk in full sentences. If not, slow down.

seo.heading: What is Zone 2 training?
seo.body: Zone 2 is the easy, conversational intensity where your body mainly uses fat for fuel. It feels almost too easy – and that is the point: you can do a lot of it and still recover for your harder sessions.

seo.heading: Why does my Zone 2 pace feel so slow?
seo.body: When you start training by heart rate, Zone 2 often means slowing down a lot, especially on hills or in the heat. After a few weeks of consistent easy training your pace at the same heart rate gets faster – that is your aerobic base improving.

pace.metaTitle: Running pace calculator & race time predictor | Peakr
pace.metaDescription: Predict your 5 km, 10 km, half marathon and marathon times and get your training pace zones from one recent race. Free, no account needed.
pace.title: Pace & race predictor
pace.description: Training paces and predicted race times from a recent race.
pace.lead: Get your training pace zones and predicted race times from one recent result.
pace.intro: Enter a recent race or all-out time trial. The more recent, the better.
pace.thresholdNote: About the pace you could hold for one hour.
pace.predictionsNote: Riegel formula. Assumes you train for the distance – longer races, especially the marathon, are often slower than predicted.

seo.heading: How are race times predicted?
seo.body: The calculator uses the Riegel formula, which scales a known race time to another distance with a fatigue factor. It works best between similar distances and assumes you have trained for the longer race.

seo.heading: What are pace zones for?
seo.body: Pace zones translate your current fitness into concrete training paces – from easy runs to threshold and interval sessions. On hilly routes or hot days, heart rate is the better guide for easy runs.

swim.metaTitle: Swim CSS calculator – Critical Swim Speed & pace zones | Peakr
swim.metaDescription: Calculate your Critical Swim Speed (CSS) and swim pace zones per 100 m from a 400 m and 200 m time trial. Free, no account needed.
swim.title: Swim pace (CSS)
swim.description: Critical Swim Speed and swim zones per 100 m from a simple test.
swim.lead: Calculate your Critical Swim Speed and swim pace zones per 100 m from two time trials.
swim.guideTitle: How to do the CSS test

guide.warmUp: Warm up for 10–15 minutes with easy swimming and a few short pick-ups.
guide.swim400: Swim 400 m as fast as you can at an even pace. Note the time.
guide.recover: Recover for 5–10 minutes with very easy swimming.
guide.swim200: Swim 200 m all-out. Note the time.
guide.record: Use the same pool and push-off starts for both efforts, then enter both times below.

swim.cssNote: Roughly the pace you can sustain for about 30 minutes.

seo.heading: What is Critical Swim Speed?
seo.body: CSS is the fastest pace you can hold for a long time without tiring rapidly – similar to the threshold pace in running. It is calculated from the difference between your 400 m and 200 m times.

seo.heading: Why pace instead of heart rate in the pool?
seo.body: Heart rate reads about 10–15 beats lower in water and wrist sensors are unreliable while swimming. Pace per 100 m from your CSS is a much more dependable target for swim sets.

privacy.metaDescription: How Peakr handles your personal data on this website.
privacy.title: Privacy policy

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: This policy explains which personal data this website processes and why. It follows the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revFADP) and, where applicable, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

sections.heading: Waitlist
sections.body: If you join the waitlist we store your email address, the consent text you agreed to and the time of your sign-up. We use this only to email you about the launch of Peakr. The legal basis is your consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR). You can withdraw your consent at any time by emailing us; we will then delete your address. We delete the waitlist at the latest 12 months after launch.

sections.heading: Database hosting (Supabase)
sections.body: Waitlist sign-ups are stored with Supabase Inc. as our processor in a data centre in the EU. Supabase processes the data only on our behalf, under a data processing agreement.

sections.heading: Website hosting (Vercel)
sections.body: This website is hosted by Vercel Inc. When you visit it, Vercel processes technical data such as your IP address, browser type and the requested page to deliver the site and protect it against abuse. These logs are kept only briefly. Data may be transferred to the USA based on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and standard contractual clauses.

sections.heading: Free calculators
sections.body: The calculators run in your browser. The values you enter are not sent to us or stored.

sections.heading: Cookies and analytics
sections.body: This website uses no tracking cookies and no analytics. Fonts are served from our own domain, not from third parties.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You can ask for access to, correction or deletion of your data, restrict or object to its processing, and receive it in a portable format. You can also lodge a complaint with a data protection authority – in Switzerland the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC).
